content:
Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator, in which Epic accuses Apple of interpreting its obligations under Brazil's recently concluded App Store antitrust agreement in a restrictive manner. Here's the full story.

Some background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it now allows developers to distribute apps in Brazil through alternative app marketplaces.

The change was part of a settlement that resolved a years-long antitrust investigation triggered by a complaint from Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods that bypass Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. More details on the structure can be found here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to a report published today by the Brazilian newspaper O Globo (via MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, alleging that Apple has erected "structural, technical, and access-related barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic pointed out that, although the new Brazilian terms apply only to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "expressly covers iPadOS."

Epic is also reportedly opposing what it calls "intimidation screens" designed to discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store, as well as the current installation process, which Epic says requires nine steps compared with the six-step process Apple currently uses in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic added that Apple's initial installation process in Europe required 15 steps, and after being asked to reduce it to six, the "download abandonment rate dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "go far beyond what is necessary to calculate fees," and argued that this allows Apple to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo reports that CADE has given Apple until Monday to respond. Apple has not publicly commented.
